sentences.text: My bag is outside the door.
My phone is in my hand.
Apartment 4B.
I check the number again.
Then I knock.
A woman opens the door.
She has a blue cup in one hand.
“Andy?”
“Yes.
Hi.
I’m Andy.”
“I’m Maya.
Come in.”
I pick up my bag and follow her.
The apartment smells of coffee.
There are two chairs by the window and a small table between them.
One chair has books on it.
“Sorry about the books,” Maya says.
“Your room’s this way.”
The room is small, but it has a desk.
I put my bag beside the bed.
“Is it okay?” she asks.
“Yes.
It’s nice.”
There are other things I want to ask.
Where can I put my food?
Does the washing machine work?
Why is there a bucket in the kitchen?
But Maya’s phone rings.
She looks at the screen and turns off the sound.
“Sorry.
Work.”
“No problem.”
My bag falls over in the hall.
A shoe comes out.
We both look at it.
“Sorry.”
I push the shoe back with my foot.
“Leave it open,” she says.
“I left my bag here for a week.”
“How long have you been here?”
“Three years.”
I look at the books on the chair again.
On top is a picture of two people on a bus.
One is asleep on the other one's shoulder.
“Did you draw that?”
“Yes.”
For the first time she puts her phone down.
“It's for a page I'm making.
Look here.”
She turns the picture round.
The people have the same coat.
I see it now.
The coat goes over both of them.
“I like the man on the right,” I say.
“That's my mum.”
I look again.
She laughs.
“She really has that hat.”
The phone lights up.
Maya looks at the name.
This time she picks it up.
“Work again?”
“Yes.
They want a new picture on somebody else's page.
Mine can wait.”
She closes the book on the two people and their one coat.
We go back to the kitchen.
“Tea?” she asks.
“Yes, please.”
“Milk?”
“No, thanks.”
Good.
I can do this.
Maya puts a cup in front of me.
Then she points to the bucket.
“The kitchen tap’s broken.
Someone’s coming tomorrow, between eight and twelve.
Can you be here?
I’ve got to go to the office.”
I hear tomorrow.
I hear eight.
“Yes,” I say.
Maya picks up her phone.
“Great.
Thank you.”
I look at the bucket.
A drop of water falls into it.
Then another.
I have a meeting tomorrow at ten.
My office is forty minutes away.
Perhaps the man will come at eight.
Perhaps the work will take ten minutes.
Perhaps I should ask.
Maya starts to type.
“Sorry,” I say.
She looks up.
“Could you say that again?
The time?”
“Between eight and twelve.”
“Eight and twelve,” I repeat.
“So, maybe eleven?”
“Yes.
We don’t have an exact time.”
“Oh.
I’m sorry.
I have to leave at nine.”
Maya puts her phone down.
“Right.”
For a moment, neither of us speaks.
“I can stay until nine,” I say.
“Is that okay?”
“Not really.
He might come later.”
My face feels hot.
I look at my tea.
Then I try another question.
“Can he come in the afternoon?”
Maya looks at her phone.
“I don’t know.
Let me ask.”
She types a message.
I move my cup away from the edge of the table.
A minute later, her phone makes a sound.
“Two to four,” she says.
“I can be home then.”
“So I don’t need to stay?”
“That’s right.”
“Okay.
Sorry about that.”
“It’s okay.”
She picks up her cup.
“Just tell me when you’re not sure.”
Her phone rings again.
“I need to take this.
Make yourself at home.”
“Thanks.”
She walks towards her room.
I look at the two chairs by the window.
Then I look at the books.
“Maya?”
“Yes?”
“Can I move these?”
“Of course.
Put them on the table.”
I move the books and sit down.
My tea is still warm.
At six, I go to the small shop near our building.
I buy milk, eggs, tomatoes and some bread.
Tomorrow is a workday.
I need something for breakfast.
When I get back, Maya’s bedroom door is closed.
I can hear her talking.
I take my food into the kitchen.
There are two shelves in the fridge.
The top shelf is almost full.
There is some cheese, a bowl of rice and three small boxes.
The bottom shelf is empty.
That must be mine.
I put my milk, eggs and tomatoes on it.
Then I put the bread on the kitchen table.
Maya comes out of her room.
“Something smells good,” she says.
“The bread’s still warm.
Would you like some?”
“Yes, please.”
She gets two plates.
I open the bag.
Then she sees the fridge.
“Oh.
Is that your food on the bottom shelf?”
“Yes.
Is that okay?”
“Sorry.
I need that shelf tonight.”
My hand stops inside the bread bag.
“All of it?”
“There’s a cake coming.
It’s for someone at work.
It’s her last day tomorrow.”
“Oh.
I didn’t know.”
“I know.
I forgot to tell you.”
I look at my shopping.
“Where can I put my food?”
“Let’s see.”
She opens the fridge and moves two boxes.
“You can use the top shelf.”
I pick up the milk, but the bottle is too tall.
“It doesn’t fit.”
“Try the door.”
There is a large bottle of water in the fridge door.
“Is this yours?” I ask.
“Yes.
You can take it out.
It doesn’t need to be cold.”
I move the water and put my milk in its place.
The eggs and tomatoes fit on the top shelf.
“What about tomorrow?” I ask.
“Can I use the bottom shelf then?”
“Yes.
The cake’s leaving with me in the morning.”
“And the top shelf?”
“We can share it.”
I look at the cheese.
“So, we share the shelf, but not all the food?”
Maya smiles.
“Right.
Please ask first.”
“Okay.
You too.”
“Of course.”
The doorbell rings.
Maya runs to get the cake.
I hold the fridge open.
The white box goes in, but the door comes back against my knee.
“Too big,” I say.
Maya gets down on the floor to look.
“The box or the cake?”
We open the lid.
The cake is yellow, with a small red chair on top.
There is a lot of white paper around it.
“Why a chair?”
“The woman who's leaving sits next to me.
When she has a question, she rolls her chair over to my desk.
Sometimes she brings her whole lunch.”
I try to imagine the office tomorrow, with one less chair rolling about.
“Will someone new come?”
Maya takes a knife out of the drawer.
“On Monday I get her pages.
That's all I know.”
“And your picture?
The people on the bus?”
“I'd like to show it on Friday.
Here, hold this.”
I hold the lid while she cuts the box down one side.
We fold the paper in.
This time the fridge door closes.
“Good,” Maya says.
“My first design today that everyone likes.”
“Ask the cake in the morning.”
We sit by the window with our bread.
A drop of water falls into the bucket in the kitchen.
“Tomorrow afternoon,” Maya says.
“Between two and four,” I reply.
She nods.
I pass her another piece of bread.
“This is for both of us.”
The next morning, the cake leaves the apartment in a large white box.
Maya holds it with both hands.
“Can you get the door?” she asks.
I open it for her.
There is space in the fridge again.
At work, my meeting finishes late.
I eat a sandwich at my desk.
At three, Maya sends a photo.
There is a new tap in our kitchen.
The bucket is gone.
Under the photo, she writes, “Dinner at seven?
My friend Rui is coming too.”
“Sounds good,” I write.
“Where?”
She sends the name of a restaurant and a map.
It is near the station, not far from home.
At six forty, I leave work.
On the train, I look at the menu on my phone.
There are pictures of noodles, rice and fish.
I am very hungry.
Then another message arrives.
“Sorry.
Still at work.
Can we make it half past seven?”
I look at the train map.
I am almost there.
I start to write, “No problem.”
Then I stop.
I am hungry.
Waiting is a small problem.
I can say that.
“I’m almost there,” I write.
“Can I order something first?”
“Yes, please do.
Rui is nearby.
I’ll ask him to meet you.”
Outside the station, there are two exits.
I choose the wrong one.
Across the road, I can see the restaurant’s green sign.
There is no crossing near me.
My phone rings.
“Hi, is that Andy?
It’s Rui.
Where are you?”
“Outside the station.”
“Which exit?”
I look behind me.
“Exit two.
There’s a flower shop.”
“Okay.
Stay there.
I’m coming.”
Five minutes later, a man in a grey jacket raises his hand.
“Andy?”
“Yes.
Thanks for finding me.”
“No problem.
The crossing is this way.”
We walk to the restaurant together.
Rui works with software too.
He knows Maya from a design course.
We start in English because he asks about the messages in our dinner group.
I want to keep trying.
Inside, we find a small table.
“Shall we wait?”
Rui asks.
“For the main food, yes.
But I’d like something small now.”
“Good.
Me too.”
We order a plate of dumplings.
Rui asks me about my new room.
I tell him about the fridge, the cake and the tap.
I forget the word for the thing under the old tap.
“It holds water,” I say.
“On the floor.”
“A bucket?”
“Yes.
A bucket.”
Rui looks at the door every time it opens.
I wonder if he wants Maya here as much as I do.
Without her, neither of us knows quite what to say.
“Do you eat here often?” I ask.
“Once.
I came with my sister.
She says the soup is good.”
“Was it?”
“I don't know.
She didn't give me any.”
He puts two bowls on the table.
We order one soup to share.
When it comes, there's one long green thing in it.
Rui tries to cut it with a spoon.
My bowl slides away across the table and I catch it with both hands.
“Perhaps your sister tried,” I say.
His laugh is so loud that a woman at the next table turns to look.
He tells me his sister always orders for the whole family.
He likes it until she orders fish.
He hates fish.
I look at the fish on the menu.
I nearly asked for it for the table.
“Can I order my own when Maya gets here?” I ask.
“Please.
You can have all the fish in the kitchen.”
“Next time we get two bowls of that,” Rui says.
I put my spoon down.
There is going to be a next time.
At seven thirty-five, Maya arrives with her laptop bag.
“Sorry I’m late.”
“We started without you,” Rui says.
“I can see that.”
There is one dumpling left.
I move the plate towards her.
“This one’s yours.”
She sits down and takes it.
“Thank you.
How was your day?”
I could say, “Fine.”
It is a good, safe word.
Instead, I tell them about the meeting that took too long, and the sandwich that was too small.
When the waiter arrives, I am still talking.
On Saturday, Rui and I meet for lunch.
There is a small café near the river.
The tables outside are full, so we sit by the kitchen door.
“English menu?” the waiter asks.
“Yes, please,” I say.
Rui looks up from his phone.
“Still practising?”
“A little.”
“Okay.
You order.”
The café has sandwiches, soup and coffee.
I choose a chicken sandwich and a hot tea.
Rui wants soup and a cold coffee.
When the waiter comes back, I tell him our order.
He says it again.
I hear the food, but a loud machine starts in the kitchen.
I miss the drinks.
I nod.
Ten minutes later, two cold coffees arrive.
I look at the glass in front of me.
There is ice inside.
“Did you want coffee?”
Rui asks.
“No.
Tea.”
“Tell him.”
The waiter is carrying plates to another table.
He looks busy.
“It’s okay,” I say.
“I can drink this.”
“You can.
But is it what you want?”
I look at the glass again.
It is a small thing.
I do not want to make it a big thing.
But I also do not want a cold coffee.
When the waiter passes our table, I raise my hand.
“Excuse me.”
“Yes?”
“I ordered a hot tea.
This is coffee.”
He looks at the small screen in his hand.
“I have two coffees here.”
For a moment, I think that is the end of the conversation.
The screen says coffee.
There is coffee on the table.
Rui waits.
He does not speak for me.
“Maybe we didn’t hear each other,” I say.
“Could I have tea instead?”
“Of course.
I’ll change it.”
“Thank you.
Do I need to pay for both?”
“No.
Just the tea.”
He takes the glass away.
My hands are warm, but not from a drink.
Rui opens his soup.
“That was fine,” he says.
“I wasn’t sure what to say.”
“You said it.”
The waiter brings a cup of tea and puts it carefully beside my sandwich.
“Hot tea,” he says.
“Yes.
Thank you.”
We eat.
Rui tells me about a problem at work.
I understand some of it.
When he speaks too fast, I ask him to slow down.
He does, but only for a minute.
Then he gets excited and goes fast again.
“Wait,” I say.
“What happened after the test?”
He puts down his spoon and starts again from there.
His phone lights up beside his bread.
There is a voice message.
Rui puts it to his ear, then plays it again.
His spoon stays in the air.
“Cold soup soon,” I say.
“Listen to this bit.
What time does he say?”
A man's voice comes out of the phone.
He speaks English very fast.
I hear a train in the background.
The man says something about a test, then something about a file.
“Five?” I say.
“That's what I hear.
Or file.
He's going home soon.
I need to know if he tried the new file.”
I push the phone back across the table.
“You can ask him.”
Rui looks at me.
I look at my tea.
We both start laughing.
He holds the phone close.
“Sorry, it's loud here.
Did you try the new file?
A text is fine.”
We eat.
His soup is cold now.
He eats it anyway.
When his friend writes back, there are just four words on the screen.
“Old file.
Trying again.”
“So when is the test?” I ask.
“He never said five.”
Rui puts his phone in his pocket.
“Five is when I want to go home.”
For a minute we can hear the river through the open door.
Later, the bill has one coffee and one tea on it.
I check the numbers and pay my part.
Outside, the river is grey.
A child is trying to fly a small kite.
It falls into the grass.
He picks it up and runs again.
“Same time next week?”
Rui asks.
“Maybe.
Send me a message.”
I put my phone away.
We walk towards the station, and this time I know which exit to use.
Two weeks later, Rui helps me carry a second-hand desk lamp home.
The lamp is cheap, but heavy.
We take turns holding it on the stairs.
“Tea?” I ask outside our door.
“Yes.
Thanks.”
His phone says ten to nine.
We planned to be home before eight, but Rui had to wait for a man to look at his washing machine.
Then the bus driver asked us to take the lamp off the empty seat.
“It needs a ticket,” Rui said to me.
I laughed all the way up the stairs.
Now I want him to sit in the chair by the window and tell me the rest of his story.
He gave me his evening.
I want to give him something too.
I open the door.
The apartment is dark except for a light under Maya’s bedroom door.
I put the lamp in my room.
Rui sits by the window.
We start talking about a film, first quietly, then louder.
He tells me about a strange scene.
I laugh.
Maya opens her door.
She is wearing headphones.
“Oh, hi, Rui.”
“Hi.”
She looks at me.
“Andy, can we talk for a minute?”
We go into the kitchen.
“I just finished a work call,” she says.
“I can hear you in my room.”
“Sorry.
We can be quiet.”
“I need the apartment to be quiet tonight.
I have another call soon.”
I look at the cups in my hands.
“Rui helped me carry something.
I only asked him in for tea.”
“I understand.
But you didn’t ask me.”
“They asked me to say my last bit again.
We ran out of time.
Now I have to send the pictures with notes tonight.”
She shows me a page with three little empty boxes under it.
“I wanted to show them this one myself.”
Her voice is tired.
Mine gets a little louder.
“I live here too.”
“Yes,” she says.
“You do.”
Neither of us speaks.
From the other room, I hear Rui move his chair.
Maya takes off her headphones.
“I’m not saying you can’t have friends here.
I’m asking you to check first when it’s late.”
I look at the clock.
It is nearly nine.
We spent longer in the lamp shop than I thought.
“Okay,” I say.
“I’m sorry about the noise.”
“Thank you.”
“We can go to the café downstairs.”
“That would help.”
Before she leaves the kitchen, I ask another question.
“What time is late?”
She stops.
“Good question.
After eight on a work night?”
“Can you check with me too?”
“Yes.
Of course.”
“And on weekends?”
“Let’s talk about that tomorrow.
I really need to get back.”
I nod.
This time, I know what I am agreeing to.
In the living room, Rui is already putting on his jacket.
“Shall we go?” he asks.
“Yes.
Sorry.”
“Don’t worry.
I need food more than tea.”
Downstairs, we order two bowls of noodles.
I tell Rui I feel bad.
“About the noise?”
“And about asking you to leave.”
“You’re coming with me,” he says.
“It’s fine.”
The next morning, Maya is at the kitchen table.
There is coffee in her blue cup.
“Thanks for last night,” she says.
“Sorry again.”
“We should make a plan.
For both of us.”
We agree to send a message before bringing visitors in the evening.
If one of us needs quiet, we will say so.
On weekends, we will check when someone wants to stay late.
Maya looks at the lamp in my room.
“That’s nice.”
“It’s very heavy.”
“Then I’m glad Rui helped.”
I switch it on.
The light falls across my empty desk.
“Would you like some tea?” I ask.
“Not now.
I’m going out.”
“Okay.
See you later.”
I make one cup and take it to my room.
A few weeks after I move in, I arrive at work and find a message on my screen.
“Team meeting.
Ten o’clock.
Please come to the meeting room.”
There is no list of topics.
Our manager, Wei, is already there.
Usually, he has coffee.
Today, he has a glass of water and several sheets of paper.
The meeting is in Chinese.
I understand every word.
For once, language is not the problem.
The company is closing our team.
There is not enough work for everyone.
Our last working day will be at the end of next month.
We will receive the details in writing.
Someone asks about pay.
Someone else asks about moving to another team.
Wei answers slowly.
There are no other positions for us at the moment.
I look at the small mark on the table beside my hand.
I have seen it in many meetings.
I have never looked at it this closely.
“Do you have any questions?”
Wei asks.
I shake my head.
Back at my desk, I open the same file three times.
I cannot remember what I want to change.
The woman at the next desk takes a green apple out of her bag.
She usually cuts it in two and puts half on my desk.
“Do you want some?” she asks.
“No, thanks.”
She puts the whole apple back.
A minute later I say, “Actually, yes.”
She gets the apple out again.
We stand by the sink and eat it there.
She wants to know who will answer the shop's calls after we leave.
I want to know if we still have our Thursday lunch.
Neither of us knows.
Wei comes in with his empty glass.
“Can I get to the tap?”
We move apart.
I nearly ask him about Thursday.
Instead I hold the door for him on his way out.
He has to carry all his papers with one hand.
At my desk the calendar is still open.
There is a meeting on it for the week after our last day.
I put my hand on the mouse to delete it.
It's someone else's meeting.
I leave it there.
At lunch, I send Rui a message.
“My team is closing.”
He calls a minute later.
“Are you okay?”
“I don’t know.”
“When do you finish?”
“At the end of next month.”
“Do you have the details?”
“They’re sending them.”
“Read them carefully.
We can talk tonight.”
I say yes, then ask what time.
When I get home, Maya is cutting vegetables.
There is room for both of us in the kitchen now.
“How was work?” she asks.
I put my bag on the floor.
“Not good.”
She puts down the knife.
“What happened?”
I know the words in Chinese.
In English, I can only find small pieces.
“My team is closing.
Next month.
I need a new job.”
“Oh, Andy.
I’m sorry.”
I sit down.
“Did you know this was coming?”
“No.
We had less work.
But I didn’t know.”
“Do you want to talk, or do you want some food first?”
“Food, please.”
She takes another plate from the cupboard.
We eat rice and vegetables.
For a while, we talk about nothing important.
She tells me the shop downstairs has new opening hours.
I tell her the lift makes a strange sound.
After dinner, I open my banking app.
I have some savings.
I can pay my part of the rent for several months, but I need to spend less.
“I can still pay the rent,” I tell Maya.
“Okay.
Thank you for telling me.”
“I’ll look for work this weekend.”
“What kind of work?”
“Software.
Maybe an international company.”
I almost laugh after saying it.
“My English isn’t good enough.”
“For every job?” she asks.
“I don’t know.”
“Then look at a few.
Find out what they need.”
She does not promise to find me a job.
She does not say everything will be easy.
She gets her laptop and begins her own work.
At eight, Rui calls.
I take the call in my room, under the light of my new lamp.
Before we finish, I write three things on a piece of paper: read the company letter, update my CV, choose three jobs to look at.
The list does not solve the problem.
But tomorrow morning, I know where to start.
The woman across the table turns her paper cup between her hands.
Behind her, someone opens the café door, and cold air moves around our feet.
“So, Andy, what do you do?” she asks.
My team closed a month ago.
Since then, my days have filled with job websites, applications, and careful trips to the supermarket.
This morning I take my old lunch box out of the cupboard, fill it, and put it straight into the fridge.
For a moment I feel ready to leave for work.
On the first Monday after the team closed, I even put my keys in my pocket before I remembered there was nowhere to go.
Rui asked me to coffee twice before I said yes.
The first time I said I was busy.
The second time he sent me a photo of the prices outside the café.
I didn't tell him about the money.
He must have noticed how often I say, “Maybe next week.”
Now there's a coffee in front of me.
I've paid for it myself.
I wish she'd asked me five minutes later.
I know this question.
I have practised an answer on the metro.
But now I look at the wet mark under my cup.
“I'm between jobs,” I say.
“Oh.”
She waits.
“My team closed.”
She looks sorry, and I want to change the subject.
Before I can ask about her work, Rui returns with three glasses of water.
“Andy builds software,” he says.
“We met through Maya.”
The woman leans forward.
Her name is Jo.
Rui met her at a local technology event, and today she is joining us for coffee.
She manages a small training business.
We use English because it is the language everyone at our table shares.
“What kind of software?” she asks.
“Business systems.
Things people use at work.”
I stop again.
My answer sounds like a box with nothing inside it.
“Can you give me an example?”
I put my cup down.
“At my last company, I worked on a stock system.
A shop could see how many products it had.”
“Like how many blue shirts?”
“Yes.
Exactly.
Sometimes the number was wrong because two people changed it at the same time.
I helped fix that.”
Jo nods.
“That sounds useful.
We have a similar problem with room bookings.”
For ten minutes, we talk about two teachers trying to use one room.
She draws two small squares on a paper napkin.
I ask how the teachers book rooms now.
I understand her answer.
I even forget to worry about the word I cannot remember.
Then she asks, “Are you looking for the same kind of role?”
“Yes, but perhaps in an international team.”
“Why?”
The easy answer is better pay.
That is part of it.
My rent does not stop when my job stops.
But there is another reason.
“I want to work with people in different places.
And I want to learn how other teams build things.”
Rui drinks his water.
He does not add anything this time.
Jo folds the napkin and puts it in her pocket.
She does not offer me a job.
I do not expect one.
Still, our conversation feels different from the forms I fill in alone.
On the way out, Rui stays behind to ask Jo about her last job.
Outside, I ask him why.
“Because I'm thinking of leaving mine.”
“But you have a job.”
“Yes.
And I get to want a different one.”
He pulls his coat shut.
“I haven't decided yet.”
I nearly tell him how lucky he is.
Then I remember sitting in the café, wishing Jo would ask about something besides the empty place on my CV.
“What would you like to do in your next job?”
We miss the first green light talking about it.
On the metro home, I open one of those forms on my phone.
Under ‘Current position’, there is an empty box.
I have looked at it three times today.
At home, Maya sits at the kitchen table with a large sheet of paper and several colour samples.
“Can I use this end?” I ask.
“Of course.
Please keep drinks away from these.”
I put my tea on the kitchen counter.
Then I open my laptop and write ‘Software developer’ in a draft of my introduction.
Under it, I describe the stock problem in three short sentences.
Maya moves a green sample beside a grey one.
“How was coffee?” she asks.
“I talked about my work.”
“Good coffee conversation?”
“Yes.
Better than my job applications.”
She smiles, but her phone rings before she can answer.
She takes the call into her room and closes the door.
I read my three sentences aloud, quietly.
The second sentence is too long.
I cut it in two.
Beside my laptop is the budget I made this morning.
I still need a job.
But when the form asks what I do, I finally have something clear to put in the box.
Two weeks after coffee with Rui and Jo, I find a role that interests me.
Maya is washing a lunch container when I come into the kitchen with my laptop.
“Could you look at my CV?” I ask.
“Just a small favour.”
She turns off the tap.
It no longer leaks, but I still sometimes expect to hear a drop.
“How long is it?”
“Four pages.”
“And when do you need it?”
“Tonight, if possible.”
She looks at the laptop, then at the clock above the fridge.
“I can't do tonight.
I have work to finish.”
“Only the English,” I say quickly.
“That can take quite a while, Andy.”
My hands tighten around the computer.
“Right.
Sorry.”
“I can give you twenty minutes tomorrow, after dinner.
Choose the part you most want help with.”
I say yes.
This time I understand exactly what I am agreeing to.
The next afternoon, I go to the public library near our apartment.
A child at the next table is drawing a bus.
I open my CV and look at its four pages.
Every small task from my old job is there.
Some sentences are longer than the bus in the child's picture.
I save a copy before changing anything.
Then I remove old school details and several lines about tools I hardly use.
I keep the work that shows what I can do.
Near the top, I have written, ‘Excellent communication skills in an international environment.’
I look at it for a long time.
I copied the style from a sample CV.
But I have never worked in an international team.
I delete the sentence.
By dinner, I have two pages and three questions.
Maya brings her bowl to the sink and sets a timer on her phone.
“Where shall we start?” she asks.
“The introduction.
And this example about the stock system.”
She reads without speaking.
I watch her face and try not to explain every line.
“What does ‘responsible for improvement’ mean here?” she asks.
“I found a problem and changed part of the system.”
“Then say that.
What problem?”
“When two workers saved new numbers together, one change could disappear.”
“Did you fix it alone?”
“No.
Another developer checked my plan, and our tester helped us check the result.”
I write that down.
The new version is longer, but it tells the truth.
Maya points to another sentence.
“You say you led the project.
Were you the project lead?”
“Not officially.
I handled that part.”
“Then perhaps say which part you handled.”
I move the cursor.
For a moment, I want to keep the stronger word.
Other applicants probably have better English and more important titles.
Then I imagine someone asking me to explain that title in an interview.
I change it.
The timer makes a soft sound.
Maya puts her hands on the edge of the table.
“I need to stop now.”
“There is one more page,” I begin.
Then I close it.
“Thanks.
I can work on the rest.”
She gathers her things.
“I can help with clear writing, but I don't know which technical details an employer needs.
Rui may know more about that.”
At the door she stops.
“Can I leave my big sheets on the table tomorrow morning?”
My first thought is of my laptop and the good chair and the light from the window.
Then I remember whose drawings I move every morning.
I always put them in a neat pile.
I have never asked if the order matters.
“Do you need them side by side?”
“Yes.
I need to see the whole thing.
At work they only show me one page at a time.”
“Leave them out.
I'll eat in the kitchen.”
She comes back with three long sheets and puts them on the table.
I recognise the line of a bus window on one of them.
She moves the middle sheet to the end and stands back.
I want to tell her which one I like.
She hasn't asked.
“Where does this go?” I say, holding up the salt.
“Anywhere off my bus.”
I take the salt and my laptop into the kitchen.
From here I can see her hands moving the pages about in the light.
While she works, I check the job advertisement myself.
It asks for experience with business software, solving problems, and working with a team.
I mark one example for each.
I want to send the application immediately, but first I read every date and company name.
At the bottom, I find an old phone number.
I replace it with the right one, save the file, and attach it to my application.
The company is called Meridian.
Before I press send, I check the attachment once more.
I press send.
In the other room Maya moves a sheet, stops, and moves it back.
I put my lunch box on the kitchen counter for tomorrow.
Three weeks after I send my application, I arrive for an interview.
The meeting room at Meridian is smaller than I expect.
Through the glass wall, I can see a row of coats and a printer with a red light.
A woman named Sara sits opposite me.
A technical manager, Ben, joins on a screen.
His first words arrive without sound.
Sara touches a button, and suddenly his voice fills the room.
“Can you hear me now?”
“Yes,” I say.
That question is easy.
Sara sets an empty glass in front of me.
The water is on Ben's side of the table.
For a second I wait for him to pass it.
Then I remember he is a face on a screen.
I stand up and reach for it myself.
“People do that,” Sara says.
“Yesterday I asked him for a pen.”
“Still looking for one,” says Ben.
I sit down again.
Until now I have heard only the voices I gave these people at home: slow questions, long silences while I answer.
The real Ben laughs through his nose.
The real Sara has blue ink on the side of her hand.
We begin with my recent work.
I explain the stock system.
Ben asks how I stopped one change from replacing another.
I draw a simple example on the paper Sara gives me.
He asks another question, and I answer it.
For a few minutes, this feels like work I already know.
Then Sara folds her hands.
“Tell me about a time when a project didn't go as planned.”
I prepared for this question.
My answer is in a notebook inside my bag.
At home, it takes two minutes.
Here, I cannot find the first sentence in my head.
“We had a problem,” I say.
“A large problem.
But we worked hard and finished.”
“What was the problem?”
“A report.
It was slow.”
“Could you tell us what you did?”
I start from the beginning.
I describe the company, the team, and the first version of the report.
I tell them which month we began.
Ben looks down at something outside the screen.
I speak faster.
After a while, Sara gently interrupts.
“And what was your own part?”
There it is again: the thing I have still not explained.
“I checked the slow part,” I say.
“I changed how we read the data.”
“Did that solve it?”
“Partly.
We also made the first release smaller.”
“Who decided that?”
“Our manager, after I showed the test results.”
“What did you leave out of that first report?”
Ben asks.
“The monthly view.
The shop managers could still see what happened that day.”
“Did they mind?”
I remember one manager with a folded piece of paper in his shirt pocket.
Every Monday he had to read numbers from it to his boss.
We had taken away the page he needed on Mondays.
“One did.
I helped him get his numbers until the next version was ready.”
Ben looks up.
“That's a part of the story I'd like to hear.”
There are five minutes left for his questions.
I have used most of his time getting to the part he wants.
Sara writes something.
I wish I had started with that sentence.
Later, Ben describes a situation with an unhappy customer and a late delivery.
There are two words I do not know.
I understand ‘customer’ and ‘Friday’, so I answer about finishing by Friday.
He pauses.
“Actually, I'm asking what you would do if Friday was no longer possible.”
My face feels hot.
“Sorry.
I misunderstood.”
I ask him to repeat the question.
This time, I say I would check the remaining work and tell the manager what was possible.
The answer is short, but at least it answers his question.
When the interview ends, Sara explains that the recruitment team will contact me about the next step.
I thank them, take my bag, and walk past the printer.
Its red light is still on.
Outside, I stand beside a tree before opening my umbrella.
People move around me toward the metro.
My phone has a message from Rui: ‘How did it go?’
I type, ‘Terrible.’
Then I remove the word.
‘Some technical questions were fine.
I got lost in one answer.’
He replies while I am on the train.
‘Which answer?’
That evening, we talk on the phone.
I explain the slow report, including everything about the first version.
“Wait,” Rui says.
“I already know your old company.
What did you do?”
I laugh, though it is not very funny.
I try again.
“The report was too slow.
I measured the problem, changed part of it, and showed the results.
We reduced the first release.”
“What happened after that?”
“The smaller report worked.
We added the other parts later.”
“Tell them that next time.”
After the call, I open my notebook.
I do not write a beautiful new speech.
I write four short lines, leaving space between them.
Then I close the notebook and try to tell the story without looking.
The next morning I find the four lines beside my empty glass.
They fit on the back of a bus ticket.
There is room underneath for the man with the folded paper.
I put him there too.
On Monday mornings, for three weeks, I was the person he called.
I had walked into an interview for a job with customers and almost forgotten to mention a customer.
My phone lights up beside a bag of noodles.
By the time I put down the vegetables and take off my gloves, the ringing stops.
There is a number I do not recognise and a voice message.
I stand near the supermarket window and press play.
A woman says her name, something about Meridian, and then several words disappear under the sound of a passing bus.
My stomach tightens.
Perhaps they want another interview.
Perhaps they have already chosen someone else.
I listen again.
This time I hear, “arrange a short feedback call”.
There is a name at the end: Lucy.
A man beside me is trying to lift a bag of rice into his basket.
He says something to me.
I hold up one finger.
I'm still listening to the end of the message.
By the time I put the phone away, he has the rice.
My gloves are on the floor and the woman behind me is holding them out.
“Busy day?” she asks.
I have spent the whole morning waiting for one phone call.
“A little,” I say.
At the till I put back a box of strawberries.
I picked them up after hearing the word Meridian.
Until the call, I was going to buy oranges.
I feel silly standing there with both kinds of fruit, trying to guess what a woman on a phone meant.
At home, I put the frozen food away first.
Then I sit at the table with my phone.
Calling back should be simple.
I have made hundreds of calls about work in Chinese.
But in English, I cannot see where the other person's sentence is going.
I write Lucy's name on a piece of paper.
Under it, I write three things: my name, missed call, feedback time.
Maya comes in carrying a long cardboard tube.
“Big delivery?” I ask.
“Presentation prints.”
She puts the tube by her bedroom door.
“Everything okay?”
“Meridian called.
I missed it.”
“Will you call back?”
“Yes.
I'm just getting ready.”
She goes into her room.
I look at my three lines once more and press the number.
“Good afternoon, Meridian recruitment.”
“Hello.
This is Andy.
I'm returning a call from Lucy about my interview.”
“One moment, please.”
Music starts.
I breathe out.
That part is done.
Lucy comes on the line and thanks me for calling.
She speaks quickly.
I hear ‘Thursday’, ‘ten’, and ‘fifteen’.
“Yes,” I begin.
Then I stop.
“Sorry, do you mean ten fifteen, or a fifteen-minute call?”
“A fifteen-minute call at ten on Thursday.”
I write it down.
“Thursday at ten in the morning, Shanghai time?”
“That's right.
I'll send you a calendar invitation.”
“Thank you.
Is there anything I should prepare?”
“No preparation is needed.
Sara would like to share feedback from the interview.”
I look at the word ‘feedback’ on my page.
It does not tell me if the news is good.
“Will you discuss the decision then?” I ask.
“Yes, Sara will explain the outcome.”
I thank Lucy and end the call.
My hand is warm around the phone.
We spoke for less than three minutes, but I feel as if I have walked up several floors.
The calendar invitation arrives.
I check the date, time, and meeting link against my notes.
They match.
I accept it and add a reminder.
For the rest of the afternoon, I want to read meaning into every word Lucy used.
She sounded friendly.
Was that a good sign?
The call is short.
Is that a bad sign?
I open another job advertisement.
After reading the same line three times, I close it and make lunch.
Maya returns to the kitchen for water.
“Did you reach them?”
“Yes.
Feedback on Thursday.”
“Okay.”
“I don't know what it means.”
She fills her glass.
“It means you have a call on Thursday.”
Her answer is almost too simple.
But she is right about what we actually know.
I eat my noodles while she checks a message.
Then she goes back to her prints, and I return to the advertisement.
Before I start reading, I turn the phone's sound on.
I place it beside the laptop, away from the edge.
The reminder is set.
There is nothing else to do about Thursday today.
On Wednesday evening the sound I have been waiting for comes from the kitchen.
I get there so quickly that Maya looks up in alarm.
It is the timer on the oven.
“Dinner,” she says.
“Unless they are hiring potatoes.”
One of her prints is on the table under four mugs.
The corners want to roll up again.
She asks me to stand by the door and tell her which line I can read from there.
I read the big one.
She asks me to try the smaller line and I have to come two steps closer.
“That's where they'll be sitting,” she says, moving one of the mugs to mark the distance.
She gets a pencil.
For the first time since lunch, an hour goes by without my touching the phone.
When I take my plate to the sink, she is still at the table, making the small letters bigger.
At nine fifty-eight on Thursday, I join the call.
My glass of water sits beside the laptop.
Outside our apartment, someone is moving a chair across the floor.
Sara appears on the screen at ten.
“Thank you for making time, Andy.”
“Thank you for speaking with me.”
She does not spend long on small talk.
“We've decided not to take your application forward.”
I look at the small picture of myself in the corner.
My face hardly changes.
“Okay,” I say.
Sara explains that the role involves frequent calls with customers.
The team needs someone who can lead those discussions from the start.
They are not confident that I am ready for that part of this particular role.
“We did see useful technical experience,” she adds.
“Your explanation of the stock problem was clear.”
I had prepared questions, but now they seem to belong to a different person.
I take a drink of water.
“Can I ask about the project example?”
“Of course.”
“Was the example wrong, or was my explanation difficult to follow?”
“The example was relevant.
But it took us some time to understand your part and the result.
A shorter structure would help.”
I write ‘my part’ and ‘result’ on the paper in front of me.
“And the customer question?”
“You answered before you fully understood it.
You corrected that when Ben repeated it.
In a customer call, checking the question earlier would be important.”
Her voice is calm.
I want to explain how nervous I was, but that will not change what they heard.
“Thank you,” I say.
“That's useful to know.”
We end the call after twelve minutes.
I close the laptop, then open it again to save my notes.
The kitchen is quiet now.
Even the chair upstairs has stopped moving.
For lunch, I cook rice and an egg.
I eat standing by the counter until I notice what I am doing.
Then I take the bowl to the table.
In the afternoon, Rui calls.
“I didn't get it,” I tell him.
“I'm sorry.”
“They need someone who can lead customer calls now.”
“That makes sense for some roles.”
I do not want it to make sense.
I want him to say they are wrong.
But he waits, and I tell him the rest of the feedback.
Then he says, “I have some news too.
I've accepted a job at Northstar.”
For a second, I say nothing.
We were looking for work at the same time, but he already has a place to go.
“That's great,” I say.
It is true, even if another feeling sits beside it.
“When do you start?”
“Next week.
I went through the interviews last month.”
He tells me about the engineering team and the trip to the office.
I ask a few questions.
Our call becomes easier.
After we hang up, I open the message where he told me he was thinking about moving.
I count back from his start date.
He must have been waiting for his own news when he asked how my interview went.
I never asked how his went.
I pick up the phone again.
I want to send him something big and cheerful.
What comes out is smaller.
‘I forgot to ask.
Is the journey to the new place any better?’
‘One train,’ he replies.
‘A seat if the whole city stays home.’
On Friday I try the report story on my phone.
I press record and put the phone across the table.
The first time, I hear myself say “we” six times.
In the middle there's a long minute about the company.
I would turn me off too.
The next recording is so short that the shop manager disappears.
On the third try I give him one sentence.
I listen while I wash my bowl.
I can hear what the man needed, what I changed, and which part another person did.
I save that one.
On Monday morning my phone shows a picture from Rui.
His new desk has three screens and no chair yet.
Under it he writes, ‘Standing job.’
I laugh before I remember to feel sorry for myself.
I send a picture of my kitchen chair.
‘Very good chair.
Expensive delivery.’
Two weeks later, he sends me a link to an open software role there.
By then, I have sent more applications and practised several work examples aloud.
‘This is a different position from mine,’ his message says.
‘You should read the requirements.
I can't promise anything.’
I open the link.
The role includes team discussions in English and some client contact with support from a project lead.
It also asks for experience I already have.
That evening, I tell Maya about it while we clear the table.
“Are you applying?” she asks.
“Yes.
But I'm checking the role carefully first.”
She hands me a dry plate.
I put it in the cupboard, then return for the next one.
My laptop waits at the far end of the table, with the new advertisement still open.
When the plates are away, I go back to the part about client calls.
I read the little word ‘with’ twice.
At Meridian they needed somebody to lead those calls immediately.
Here a project lead goes too.
I open a fresh application.
In the box about working with customers I write about the shop manager and his Monday numbers.
I leave Rui's name out of that box.
He wasn't there.
Daniel offers me water before we sit down.
Three people are waiting for me in the Northstar meeting room: Daniel, who leads project delivery, and two engineers, Mei and Omar.
I place my notebook on the table.
I know Rui works somewhere in this building, but he is not part of my interview.
Daniel begins with a short description of the role.
The team builds software for organisations with several locations.
Developers work closely with the people who use the systems.
“You've worked mostly in a local team,” he says.
“What would be new for you here?”
“Using English through the whole working day,” I say.
“I can discuss technical work, but I sometimes need a question repeated.
I haven't led regular client meetings in English.”
He nods.
“Thank you for being clear.”
Then Mei asks about a project that had problems.
This time, I do not begin with the history of my old company.
“A report was too slow for daily use,” I say.
“I measured where the time went and changed how we read the data.
That helped, but it didn't solve everything.”
“What did you do next?”
“I showed the results to our manager.
We released a smaller report first.
I worked with another developer and a tester on the remaining parts.”
Omar asks what I would measure differently now.
I need a moment, so I ask for one.
Then I explain that I would test with more realistic amounts of data earlier.
Mei turns a sheet of paper toward me.
It shows a small booking system.
Two people are trying to reserve the same room.
“How would you handle a conflict?” she asks.
I almost begin talking about disagreements between colleagues.
Then I look at the drawing.
“By conflict, do you mean two bookings for the same room and time?”
“Yes.
Both people press confirm almost together.”
I draw two arrows and explain where I would check availability.
Mei asks why checking only on the first screen is not enough.
“Because the room may become unavailable before the person confirms,” I say.
We discuss how to protect that final step.
I forget a technical word halfway through an answer.
“I can't remember the English term,” I say.
“I mean that these changes must succeed together, or none of them should remain.”
Omar supplies the word.
I thank him and continue.
The missing word does not end the discussion.
Near the end, Daniel asks if I have questions.
“What support is there for a developer who is new to client discussions?”
He explains that I would first join calls with him or another experienced colleague.
I would still need to prepare, ask questions, and give updates.
The job would not come with a personal English teacher.
“That sounds reasonable,” I say.
“How do you share decisions after a call?”
“We write them down.
Sometimes we need a reminder to do it.”
He smiles briefly, then checks the time.
Our hour is finished.
I leave tired, with no idea what their decision will be.
On the metro, I write down one question I answered badly.
Then I write down one I clarified before answering.
Over the next two weeks, I complete the remaining recruitment steps.
I have a final conversation with the hiring team and give permission for them to contact my references.
Waiting still makes it difficult to sleep some nights.
The offer arrives on a Monday afternoon.
I read the role, pay, and conditions slowly.
Then I speak with the recruiter to check the details before accepting.
My start date is three weeks away.
When Maya comes home, I am setting two plates on the table.
“I have news,” I say.
She puts down her bag.
“Good news?”
“Yes.
Northstar offered me the job.
I accepted.”
She grins and pulls out her chair.
“Tell me.”
I tell her about the money and the start date.
She asks if I am pleased.
It takes me a moment to say yes.
For weeks, every time I open my mouth to talk about work, I have to explain what happened to my old team.
I still have the start of that sentence ready.
“Did you show yours today?” I ask.
There is blue tape on the sleeve of her coat.
She takes it off and rolls it between her fingers.
“Both versions.
They chose the safe one.”
“Which one is that?”
“The one they've already seen about twelve times.”
I get up to fetch the food.
From beside the stove I ask, “Could you show the other one to—”
“Andy, I spent the afternoon hearing what I could do.”
I turn the heat down and bring the pan to the table.
“What happened when you showed them yours?”
She makes a place for the pan.
“Somebody at the back moved his chair closer.
I thought he wanted to see my drawing.
He wanted to plug in his computer.”
She gives a small laugh.
“But the woman beside him asked where I got the idea.
I did get to answer that.”
She tells me about a morning spent watching people try to read a sign from the end of a hall.
She gets up halfway through dinner to show me how far away they stood.
Her version has fewer words; you can read them without walking all the way to the wall.
“Like your print in the kitchen,” I say.
“Yes.
Exactly like that.”
When we finally eat, the rice at the bottom of the pan is brown.
We both like that part.
Maya divides it with the edge of the spoon, very carefully, as if there might be a serious argument about who gets more.
“Three weeks,” she says, passing me my share.
“You'll have to start getting up before me again.”
I had forgotten that part of having a job.
My new work card does not open the door.
I hold it against the black square again.
A red light appears, followed by a short, unfriendly sound.
“Turn it over,” says someone behind me.
Rui stands there with two paper cups.
I turn the card over.
This time the light is green.
“Excellent technical work,” he says, giving me one cup.
I laugh, although I have spent the whole train journey trying to look like a person who belongs here.
Northstar occupies one floor of an office building near a busy Shanghai road.
From the lift, I can hear drills somewhere below us.
Inside, the office smells of coffee and new carpet.
Rui shows me an empty desk with a monitor, a keyboard and a little packet of screws.
“The monitor stand needs one of those,” he says.
“Don't throw them away.”
Three weeks have passed since the offer.
I have read the documents twice, bought a notebook and checked the route.
None of that tells me what to do with my coat.
Daniel arrives while I am putting it over my chair.
He carries a laptop under one arm.
“Welcome, Andy.
Sorry, it's a busy morning.
Have you got access?”
“To the office, yes.”
He smiles briefly.
“I mean the development system.”
“Not yet.”
“IT will help.
Read the project notes, then sit with Rui.
There's a client call later.
Just listen today.”
He is already looking towards a meeting room.
“What time is the call?” I ask.
“Four thirty.
I'll send the invitation.”
His answer is perfectly ordinary.
I feel foolish for needing courage to ask the question.
By lunch, I can open the code and the team messages.
I cannot run the application.
A small error box covers the screen.
Rui leans across the space between our desks.
“Did you install the local database?”
“I followed the setup page.”
He reads it and makes a noise through his teeth.
“Old instructions.
Wait.”
I nearly apologise.
Then I stop.
The page is old; my English has not broken the database.
We find the missing step together.
I add it to the page while Rui checks that the application starts.
A calendar appears, full of imaginary classes: drawing, basic computing, English conversation.
“The client runs community learning centres,” Rui explains.
“They need one place for bookings and schedules.”
He opens a class with twelve enrolled learners.
“This part is ours.
Staff change a class time, and the system tells the learners.”
“That sounds simple.”
Rui looks at me.
“It sounds simple.”
“Can I stay beside you this afternoon?” I ask.
“Just until the call?”
Rui looks at his calendar.
“Until two.
I promised someone I'd look at their work after that.”
“I'll sit quietly.”
“You say that now.”
He turns his screen towards me.
There are already three little windows with his name in them.
“I like having you here, Andy.
I also liked having lunch.”
I notice the unopened sandwich under his monitor.
It is almost two already.
I take my notebook back to my own desk.
For a while I keep a list of everything I want to ask him.
Then I try a class change on my own.
The calendar has two classes called Drawing.
The first is full; the second has only four names.
I had assumed I was seeing the same class twice.
When I look at the details, one meets on Tuesday, the other on Thursday.
I cross out my first question.
My second is better: if staff move Tuesday's class to Thursday, how will the people reading the message know which class has moved?
I leave that one on the page.
Across the aisle Rui finally opens his sandwich.
He has cut it in half.
Someone comes over carrying a laptop before he can pick up the second half.
At four thirty, we sit in a small room.
Elena joins from London.
Behind her, a woman walks past carrying a pile of folders.
Elena asks us to wait while she finds her headphones.
Daniel introduces me.
I have prepared two sentences, but my name comes out too quietly.
Elena moves closer to her camera.
“Sorry, could you say that again?”
“I'm Andy.
I'll be working on the booking system with Rui.”
“Welcome.
I hope he hasn't shown you all our complicated spreadsheets yet.”
“Only the calendar.”
“Then there's still hope.”
Everyone laughs.
I do too, a second late.
During the call, I understand the main problem.
Centre staff currently copy changes between several lists.
But I lose a discussion about which list is the official record.
I write a question mark beside it instead of pretending I understand.
After the call, Daniel points at my notebook.
“All clear?”
My mouth starts to form yes.
“Mostly.
Which list should we use if two records disagree?”
He puts his laptop down again.
“Good question.
We haven't agreed that yet.
Don't build a rule for it.”
I underline those last words.
At home, Maya is cutting a large sheet of blue paper on the table.
Small triangles cover the floor.
“How was Monday?” she asks.
“I fixed some instructions.
Asked two questions.
Failed to open a door.”
“Busy day.”
She moves her cutting mat towards her side.
“I have a presentation tomorrow.
Can I keep this half until ten?”
“Of course.
I'll eat here.”
I point to the clear corner.
While my rice warms, I open my notebook.
Under tomorrow's date, I write the question I did not ask: what should I finish this week?
Maya reaches across the table for a piece of tape.
“What's the question?”
I read it to her.
“And who's got the answer?”
“Daniel.”
“Good.
For a moment I thought it was me.”
She sticks a paper sign to the back of a chair and walks to the hallway to look at it.
I carry my bowl around her line of sight.
In the morning, before I even take my coat off, I stop at Daniel's desk and ask him.
He wants me to take the little window that confirms a class change.
I can see the whole thing in my head.
Two buttons and a time.
I tell him I'd like to do it.
The green mark beside my task looks reassuring.
It is the third week of my new job, and I have finally finished something that other people can see.
When a staff member changes a class time, a small window asks them to confirm.
The new time then appears on the calendar.
I have checked it with several test classes.
Daniel stops beside my desk.
“Is the change-time work done?”
“Yes,” I say.
“Great.
Can I show it this afternoon?”
My hands stay on the keyboard.
“The calendar part?”
“The whole journey.
Change the time, notify the learners.”
Behind him, Rui slowly removes his headphones.
“The notification work is a separate task,” I say.
“I thought you meant mine.”
Daniel looks at the green mark.
“It says 'change class time'.”
“It does.”
He takes a breath, then looks at his watch.
“Meeting room.
Ten minutes.
Let's find out what we actually have.”
The room has a whiteboard with half a drawing left from another meeting.
Rui wipes away a square but leaves a cloud in the corner.
I bring my laptop and the uncomfortable feeling that I have passed an exam using the wrong question paper.
Daniel draws three boxes: change, save, notify.
“Where are we?”
“The change window works,” I say.
“The new time is saved.
I tested both.
But the notification service isn't connected to this screen.”
“And if saving fails?”
“The window stays open and shows an error.”
“What does the error say?”
I show him.
The message says that the action could not be completed.
“Does it tell staff whether the old time is still there?”
Rui asks.
“No.
It should.”
Daniel taps the third box.
“Can we connect this by lunch?”
Rui looks at me, but does not answer for me.
“I can connect it,” I say slowly.
“I can't say it's ready for a demonstration until we check the result.”
“What result?”
“Whether the email shows the correct old and new times.
And whether only people enrolled in that class receive it.”
Daniel puts down the pen.
“All right.
That's more useful than just saying no.”
I want to explain that I am not saying no at all.
Instead, I turn my laptop so we can all see the task description.
“Could we agree what 'done' means here?”
There is a brief silence.
I hear a trolley rolling along the corridor.
Daniel pulls the keyboard towards him.
“Yes.
Let's write it now.”
We make a short checklist.
A valid new time must be saved.
If saving fails, the old time must remain and the screen must explain that.
A notification must show both times clearly.
The test must use enrolled test learners, not every name in the database.
Rui adds another line: another engineer must review the change.
“Me?” I ask.
“Not your own change,” he says.
“I'll review yours.
You'll review mine when you've learnt more of the system.”
Daniel deletes the green mark and replaces it with 'in progress'.
My face warms, though nobody comments.
“Today's demonstration?” I ask.
“I'll show the calendar and explain that notifications are still being tested,” he says.
“I should have checked before promising the whole journey.”
That helps, but it does not remove my part.
I chose the word done because it was short and sounded confident.
I could have described exactly what worked.
After the meeting, Rui returns to his desk.
I follow him.
“Was my answer very bad?”
“It was incomplete.”
He pulls out his chair.
“Those aren't always the same thing.”
He shows me a task he completed the previous month.
Under its checklist are three comments and a photograph of a handwritten calculation.
“I missed a case,” he says.
“A reviewer found it.”
I read the comments.
They are direct, but none says that Rui is a bad engineer.
Later, I change the error message and run the saving tests again.
Then I write an update: 'Calendar change and save are working in the test environment.
Email connection and review are still outstanding.'
It takes longer than typing done.
Daniel replies with a thumbs-up and moves his demonstration to the smaller scope.
Before I leave, I take one final look at the task.
The mark is still grey.
For once, the colour is telling the truth.
Just as I reach for my coat, Daniel calls me back.
He has finished the smaller demonstration.
Someone from a centre has stayed on the line with a question about the calendar.
Would I take it?
On his screen a woman is sitting in a room with a coat over the back of the next chair.
She has written the two class times on a scrap of paper.
“Suppose I save the new time and the phone rings,” she says.
“I turn to answer it.
When I get back, how do I know whether anybody's been told?”
I have been thinking about the person who stays in front of the screen until the job is finished.
It hasn't occurred to me that this person also answers the phone.
“In the version you saw today, nobody gets an email,” I say.
“You would still have to contact people yourself.”
“Yes, I gathered that.
I'm asking about the version we're waiting for.”
Daniel starts to speak, then looks at me.
I could describe the email connection we mean to build.
That still wouldn't answer her question.
“I don't know what you'll see when you come back to the desk,” I say.
“Could we bring that question to the staff demonstration?”
“Please do.
You'll have people there who spend a lot of time being interrupted.”
As if on cue, someone off screen asks her where the spare pens are.
“Second drawer,” she says, without turning her head.
On the way out, Daniel holds the door for me.
“I almost told her the email would have both times in it.”
“So did I.”
He takes out his phone and adds her words to the invitation draft.
For once the thing we need to show somebody is the moment after the part we planned to show.
On Thursday afternoon, an invitation arrives with the title 'Friday demo'.
I open it while waiting for a test to finish.
It shows a time in the late afternoon, so I accept and return to my code.
Five minutes later, Daniel sends a message: 'Need the version ready by Friday morning.'
I type 'Sure'.
Before I send it, I look again at the invitation.
It has no explanation of what ready means.
The meeting includes Elena in London and several people I have never met.
Friday morning where?
I delete my answer and walk to Daniel's desk.
He is speaking into his headset, drawing circles in the air with one finger.
I wait at a distance until he looks up.
“Two minutes,” he says, covering the microphone.
I point at the small kitchen and go to fill my water bottle.
The machine makes a long noise before giving me half a cup.
By the time I return, Daniel has ended his call.
“About Friday morning,” I say.
“Do you mean Shanghai time or London time?”
“London.
Elena wants to check the demonstration before the staff session.”
“So there are two sessions?”
He looks at his calendar.
“You've only got the second invitation?”
I show him my screen.
“Right.
I missed you off the first.”
For a moment I feel pleased that the confusion is not entirely mine.
Then he opens another message, and I notice a different date.
“This says next Friday,” I say.
“That's the staff session.
The check with Elena is tomorrow.”
I sit in the empty chair beside him.
“Could we put both dates and both time zones in one message?”
Daniel rubs his eyes.
“Please do.
Send it to me before it goes out.”
At my desk, I open the calendar's world clock rather than calculate from memory.
The London offset changes during the year, and I do not want yesterday's guess to become today's appointment.
For these dates, the calendar shows London eight hours behind Shanghai.
I write two lines.
The first is a short check with Elena this Friday at nine in the morning London time, five in the afternoon Shanghai time.
The second is the staff demonstration on the following Friday, at the same local times.
I include the full calendar date on each line.
Then I add a third sentence: 'Both sessions use the test environment and test learner accounts.'
Rui reads it over my shoulder.
“Add that neither session is a launch.”
“Would anyone think that?”
“Someone wrote 'ready Friday'.
Someone else might forward it.”
I add the sentence.
Daniel approves the message and corrects both invitations.
Elena replies with a thank-you and one question: can staff try changing a class themselves during the second session?
That question changes our preparation.
A demonstration I control is different from six people clicking buttons.
Rui and I book time to reset the test classes, check permissions and prepare separate accounts.
We also choose one sample class to use if the system is slow.
Daniel asks whether we need a recording as a backup.
“A few screenshots would be quicker,” I say.
“They can explain the steps, but they won't prove the live test is working.”
“Fine.
Label them clearly.”
By Friday afternoon, the screenshots are ready.
So are the test accounts.
I join the call ten minutes early and discover that I cannot share the application window.
I leave and rejoin after changing a permission, grateful that Elena is not yet waiting.
At five, her face appears.
“Good morning,” I say, then laugh.
“Your morning.”
“Good afternoon to you.
Shall we start with what staff will see?”
We change a test class from ten to eleven.
The notification arrives in a test inbox.
Elena reads it silently.
“Could the old time be easier to notice?” she asks.
I write that down.
We have time to adjust the layout before the staff demonstration.
We do not have to pretend the first version is final.
When the call ends, Daniel asks if I can stay late next Friday in case the staff session runs over.
“I can stay until six,” I say.
“After that, I have an appointment.”
“Rui?”
Daniel asks.
“I'm helping my family on Friday evening.
I have to leave at six too.”
Daniel studies the invitation again.
“I thought I had the two of you until the end.”
“You have both of us until six,” Rui says.
“What do you actually need at the end?”
Daniel counts on his fingers.
He wants people to change a class, read the message, and talk about what to do if a learner calls.
The last part is where he expects difficult questions.
If he leaves it to the end, the people he wants in the room may already be on the train.
“Then why save it for last?” I ask.
“Because it's the conversation I can't put a time on,” he says.
He looks down at his fingers.
“Which is an excellent reason to start it earlier.”
He moves the support discussion earlier.
On the train home, my phone shows the two invitations beside each other.
Same title, different dates, clear descriptions.
I close the calendar and send Maya a message that I will be home for dinner.
The following Friday, a woman at one of the centre desks changes the time of a test class.
Then she pushes her chair away from the screen.
“Pretend the phone has just rung,” she says.
A man beside her picks up a folded sheet of paper and holds it to his ear.
He does such a good front-desk voice that someone at the other end of the call tries to answer him.
When she comes back, she finds the new time easily.
What she wants next is the list of people who should hear about it.
We can show her test names.
She recognises none of them, of course, and she laughs at herself for trying.
“Next time,” she says, “could you show us how you know you have the right list?”
It's a fair question.
We have made these accounts ourselves.
There is a whole step between a list we wrote and a list held by the centre.
At six Rui stands up with his coat on.
My hand is already on the lid of my laptop.
Daniel catches my eye and points at the door.
He stays to collect the final questions.
This time the invitation has been right about the end as well as the beginning.
The waiting circle turns for so long that I begin to watch it instead of the clock.
Then the request fails.
I try again with the same test account, and the same red message appears.
It is several weeks after the staff demonstration.
We have changed the notification layout and collected more questions from the centres.
Now I am connecting our work to the client's test service, which provides enrolment information.
Without that information, we cannot reliably check who should receive a changed-time email.
Beside my keyboard is a page from the staff demonstration.
At the top I have written a question from the woman who answered an imaginary phone: How do you know you have the right list?
This morning Mei offered to sit with me and compare the two lists once the connection was ready.
She set aside the hour before lunch.
At eleven thirty she came over carrying a banana and her notebook.
“Still a good time?”
“Give me ten minutes.”
She peeled the banana.
We watched the circle turn.
By the time she dropped the skin into the bin, I was back at the same red message.
“I have to go,” she said.
“Someone needs me to look at the calendar.
Tell me when you've got something I can compare.”
Now the empty chair beside me is bothering me more than the red message.
She could have spent that half hour somewhere else.
Yesterday, I thought the connection problem would take an hour.
This morning, I thought it would be fixed before lunch.
It is now two fifteen.
Our team update starts at three.
I open the request details again.
Access denied.
Perhaps I have missed something obvious.
Perhaps everyone else would know what to change.
Rui rolls his chair back.
“Coming for coffee?”
“In a minute.”
“You said that an hour ago.”
“I need to fix this first.”
He looks at the screen.
“How long has it been blocked?”
“Since yesterday afternoon.”
“Does Daniel know?”
“He knows I'm working on the connection.”
“That isn't the same thing.”
The words annoy me because they are true.
I turn towards him.
“I don't want to report a problem I should be able to solve.”
Rui puts his mug down.
“Report what you've checked.
Then we can decide whether it's yours to solve.”
We spend ten minutes comparing the request with the client's instructions.
The address is correct.
The account name is correct.
A basic connection succeeds, but the enrolment request is refused.
I have enough facts to describe the problem, even if I do not have its answer.
I send Daniel a short message before the update.
He replies, 'Bring that first.'
At three, five of us gather around a table.
Daniel opens a list of tasks.
My name is halfway down, but he looks at me immediately.
“What's blocking the connection?”
“The client test service refuses our enrolment request.
I've checked the address and account details.
The basic connection works, so the service is reachable.”
“What's the impact?”
“We can continue testing the screen with local data.
We can't verify the full journey with the client's test records.”
“Can you finish tomorrow?”
I press my thumb against the edge of my notebook.
“I can finish my checks tomorrow.
I can't promise the connection will work until we know why access is refused.”
Daniel looks unhappy.
“I told Elena we'd have an update this week.”
“We can give her an update,” Rui says.
“We just can't call the full test complete.”
Daniel turns back to me.
“What do you need?”
“A contact who can check the account permissions.
And someone to confirm which test classes we are allowed to use.”
He writes both items down.
“I'll ask Elena for the right contact today.
You send the facts, without passwords or keys.”
I nod.
Then I add something I would rather leave out.
“I should have raised it yesterday.
I kept expecting the next attempt to work.”
“Yes,” Daniel says.
“Next time, tell me sooner.
Waiting doesn't make the dependency smaller.”
There is no angry speech.
We move to another person's task.
I feel exposed for several minutes, and then strangely able to work again.
Afterwards, I prepare a short note with the failed request time, the error message and the checks already completed.
I remove account secrets before sharing it.
I also list what we can still test locally.
Elena replies before I leave.
She gives us a service contact, but that person cannot inspect the permissions until the next day.
It is not the quick rescue I hoped for.
Daniel asks me to adjust the task estimate and mark the external dependency.
We agree on another update tomorrow at four, even if the problem remains unresolved.
At home, Maya is listening to a recording through headphones.
She holds up one finger when I come in.
I put my bag down and start washing rice.
A few minutes later, she joins me.
“Hard day?”
“I spent most of it wanting a better answer.”
“Did you get one?”
“Not yet.
But other people know the actual question now.”
The rice slips between my fingers into the bowl.
I turn off the tap before the water reaches the top.
The next afternoon at four I still cannot open the records.
I call Mei first.
I owe her at least that much.
“Have you kept another hour for me?” I ask.
“No.
Should I have?”
“Good.
No.
The person on the client side is checking which classes the account can see.
I'll ask for your time when there's a list in front of me.”
“Andy?”
“Yes?”
“Yesterday I wasn't sitting there because I thought you were slow.
You said ten minutes.
I believed you.”
There is no answer I can give that will give her the time back.
“I know.
I'm sorry.”
“Okay.
Send me a picture of that list when you get it.
A picture of test names,” she adds.
“You can keep the red circle.”
At five past four, Daniel has my update and Mei is at somebody else's desk.
The chair beside me stays empty.
Today that feels right.
Six messages arrive in the test inbox while I am looking at a single class.
Each subject line announces the same new time.
I refresh the page, hoping that the inbox is showing one message several times.
It is not.
Rui stands behind my chair.
We have been running an internal test of repeated class changes.
The connection problem from last month has been resolved, and the test service now provides the records we need.
Today should have been straightforward.
“How many times did you change it?” he asks.
“Three.”
“Then why are there six emails?”
I open the logs.
My chest feels tight before I find the answer.
The first change creates one notification.
The second sends two.
The third sends three.
Each time, my code creates a new job from the earlier change records as well as the current one.
I wrote it that way.
I remember thinking that learners might need another reminder of earlier changes.
I did not ask anyone whether that was wanted.
I did not properly consider how the same path would run each time a class was edited.
“Stop the test,” I say.
Rui closes the test screen.
I pause the notification jobs for our internal environment.
Then we check the addresses against the test account list.
Every message has gone to an inbox controlled by our team.
No real learner or centre staff member has received one.
That matters.
It does not make the code right.
Daniel joins us after reading Rui's message.
“Is this the email service sending twice?”
“No,” I say.
The word comes out too sharply.
I try again.
“No.
It's my change logic.
I create jobs for previous changes again.
I assumed we wanted repeated notices without checking.”
“Who received them?”
“Only our internal test accounts.
We've checked the recipients.”
“And is it still running?”
“I've paused these test jobs.”
He pulls over a chair.
“Show me.”
I show him the three actions and six messages.
We write down the times, the affected test class and the number of jobs.
Rui checks my explanation against the logs rather than accepting it because I sound certain.
Daniel asks how long the repair will take.
“The code change may be small,” I say.
“I need to check the rule with Elena and test repeated edits before I estimate the whole repair.”
He looks at the calendar.
“We were planning to finish this review tomorrow.”
“I know.”
I want to offer to work all night.
It would sound like taking responsibility.
It would also be another promise made before I understand the work.
We send Elena a short explanation of the internal failure and a specific question about repeated changes.
Her reply is clear: each saved time change should produce its own notification showing that change.
Earlier changes should not be sent again simply because staff edit the class later.
Repeating a failed delivery is a separate technical case, not a new change notice.
With that rule written down, Rui and I work through the fix.
I remove the loop over earlier changes from the new-change path.
We add checks for two and three consecutive edits, and for a job that is attempted again after a temporary failure.
We also check that saving the same unchanged time does not create another change notice.
The first new test fails.
I have fixed the normal path but missed another place where jobs are created.
Rui points to it without speaking.
I feel my face heat up again and make the second correction.
By late afternoon, the automated checks pass.
We reset the test class and repeat the internal exercise together.
Three saved changes produce three notices with the expected times.
Repeating the same job does not add a duplicate message in our controlled test.
Daniel moves the review by two days so another engineer can examine the change and the wider notification flow.
Passing our checks is useful evidence; it is not the end of the investigation.
Rui is still at the printer when I leave.
A drawing of his own test is coming out in pieces.
He lines the sheets up on the floor with his shoe.
“Is that for tomorrow?”
“It was for today.
I gave my slot to the review.”
I offer to stay and run it for him.
He shakes his head.
“Andy, you don't know this part.
It would take half the evening to explain.”
I stand there with my coat on.
It would feel better if he would give me something hard to do.
He points at the last sheet.
“You could pick that up.
If I move my foot the whole thing goes.”
I pick it up.
Under the diagram he has written three questions in small letters.
One of them is the question neither of us asked when he reviewed my code.
“I thought you'd checked with Elena,” he says.
“I saw that line and let it go.
In front of Daniel I let you do all the talking, too.”
“It was my change.”
“Yes.
And my review.”
He rolls the pages up together.
“I'm sorry about the talking part.”
I tell him I'm sorry he lost the afternoon.
We walk to the lift together.
He presses the button twice, catches me looking and laughs for the first time since lunch.
At home Maya asks if I want company.
I sit on the kitchen floor with my back against a cupboard while she makes toast.
We share the first slice standing up because the second one burns.
For ten minutes there is something in the flat more urgent than my mistake.
Daniel writes the names of all the community learning centres across the whiteboard.
There are more than I can comfortably hold in my head.
Under them, he draws one long line and writes 'same week?'
The question mark is small.
I keep looking at it.
The notification repair has completed its additional review.
We have corrected another minor logging issue and recorded the test results.
The system is more reliable than it was, but my confidence has not returned at the same speed.
“We need a plan to discuss with Elena,” Daniel says.
“Not another list of things we might do.”
Rui turns his pen between his fingers.
“The centres have different class schedules.
Doing everything in one week will make support busy.”
“It also limits how long we maintain two ways of working,” Daniel says.
I have written a suggestion in my notebook.
The words look reasonable there, where nobody can disagree with them.
“What if we started with one centre?” I ask.
Daniel looks at me.
“As a pilot?”
“Yes.
A limited pilot.
We could watch the actual work more closely and find problems before involving all the centres.”
“And how long would that take?”
“I don't know yet.
We'd need to agree what we're trying to learn and how the centre would take part.”
Daniel leans back.
“I'm willing to consider it, but we can't keep calling uncertainty a plan.”
I close the notebook halfway, then open it again.
“Could I compare the options for the client discussion?
Including the extra work a pilot creates?”
He considers this.
“By tomorrow afternoon.
Keep it short.”
Rui and I take the small meeting room after lunch.
Instead of starting with a presentation, we draw the current staff journey: find the class, change the record, tell learners, check whether anyone needs more help.
“Whose job is this last part?” I ask.
“Probably centre staff.”
Rui turns my notebook round.
“Let's try it.
I'll be a tutor.
You're on the desk.
My room's full of chairs with wet paint.
I need the other room.”
“That's a very strange centre.”
“Excellent chairs.
Terrible planning.”
I change the room on a sheet of paper.
He holds out his hand for the other sheet.
I haven't touched it.
“Somebody at your old desk still thinks I'm teaching among the chairs,” he says.
We try again.
This time I remember both sheets, but when he asks which one I changed first I can't tell.
It takes thirty seconds for two people who made up the problem to lose track of it.
I cross out easy to manage.
Under the three choices I write what each would ask of a person alone at a desk.
If we introduce the system everywhere, everybody learns at once.
If we wait, everybody keeps doing today's work.
If we choose one centre, somebody there becomes the link between two ways of working.
I can give Daniel the choices.
I don't know the name of the person who would have to live with the third one.
In the afternoon, we test another sequence of changes and a temporary notification failure.
The system records what happened, but it cannot tell us whether a learner has read an email.
I add that limitation to the draft.
Rui reads over it.
“Don't promise that fewer centres means fewer problems.”
“Fewer people exposed to the first problems?”
“If the scope really stays limited.”
I change the sentence.
The next day, I sit opposite Daniel with a single printed page.
He reads it without speaking.
I resist the urge to explain every line before he reaches it.
“You've put staff time under every option,” he says.
“It belongs under every option.”
“Fair.”
He taps the pilot column.
“Who chooses the centre?”
“Elena and the centre, I think.
We can explain the technical requirements, but we don't know their workload.”
“What would make us stop?”
