I show him a short list of proposed conditions: incorrect times, wrong recipients, or a failure staff cannot handle through an agreed fallback.
None of the conditions is approved yet.
We also need a reliable way to return to the existing process without losing changes.
Daniel draws a line under that point.
“That's not a small detail.”
“No.
We'd have to test it and agree who makes the decision.”
He looks out through the glass wall.
Someone is carrying a monitor past, walking backwards while a colleague holds the other end.
“All right,” he says.
“Let's evaluate the one-centre approach with Elena.
I'm not approving a launch date today.”
“I'll make that clear in the notes.”
“And send her the alternatives.
She may have reasons we haven't considered.”
At the printer I find my first diagram lying face up.
One centre is a little square.
I try putting my thumb over it.
A whole building disappears.
Rui comes up behind me.
“Are you doing magic?”
“Bad magic.
I can make London vanish.”
“Can you make the printer work?”
Its red light is on.
We open the tray and find the back of my proposal folded like a fan.
When I pull it straight the line about extra staff is almost impossible to read.
I write it in again with his pen.
That is the copy I keep.
Elena gets the clean version, including the option to wait.
Half an hour later a reply arrives.
She can give us twenty minutes between the end of one class and the start of another.
There is no comment about the plan.
For the first time it occurs to me that those twenty minutes already belong to somebody.
Elena moves closer to her camera.
Behind her, a door opens and somebody passes carrying a tower of plastic cups.
She waits until the door closes before speaking.
“I understand why you prefer one centre,” she says.
“What I don't understand is who does the extra work.”
On my screen, our proposal looks reassuring: a small group, fewer risks, time to learn.
I have spent the morning adjusting the arrows between its boxes.
None of the arrows represents a person missing lunch.
Daniel leans forward.
“The smaller pilot should reduce the workload.”
“For your team, perhaps.”
Elena says it gently, which makes the sentence harder to dismiss.
“Our reception team would be learning a new system while maintaining the old one.”
I close the diagram.
Rui, beside me in the Shanghai meeting room, stops turning his pen.
We had expected questions about reliability.
Instead, the first question concerns the daily cost of trying something new.
“Could you take us through a normal change?” I ask.
“Starting before anyone opens the software.”
Elena looks away to think.
“A tutor calls in sick.
A manager finds another room and another time.
Reception checks who's enrolled.
Some learners receive email.
Others need a telephone call.
Someone writes the change on the noticeboard.
Then people call back with questions.”
“Does one person handle all of that?”
“Not necessarily.
That's part of the problem.”
I write the steps down, leaving space between them.
The empty spaces are more useful than my arrows.
They give Elena somewhere to add what we have missed.
“Who decides whether a learner has been informed?” I ask.
“Sometimes nobody can tell.
A message was sent, but the learner hasn't seen it.
Or one receptionist made the call and another receptionist answers the callback.”
Rui turns towards the microphone.
“We can show whether the email service accepted a message.
We can't show that the person understood it.”
“Exactly,” Elena says.
“Please don't label that as informed.”
The word is already in a draft screen.
I put a square around it in my notes.
Daniel glances at the clock.
We have twenty minutes left, and I recognise the movement because I make it myself when a conversation stops following my plan.
He is due in another meeting.
I am due to discover how little our neat proposal contains.
“There are also learners who don't use email,” Elena continues.
“And people who use it but need information in a different form.
A small pilot cannot mean we quietly leave those people outside it.”
My first thought is a new feature: automatic calls, perhaps, or text messages.
I almost say it.
Then I remember the duplicate messages in our internal test.
A clever answer given too quickly can become a promise, and a promise can turn into somebody else's difficult afternoon.
“We haven't established what would help them,” I say.
“Would it be possible to speak to someone at reception before we choose the group?”
Elena's shoulders relax a little.
“Yes.
Priya manages the centre we're considering.
She'll tell you what is practical.”
“Could she join our next meeting?”
Daniel asks.
“Only if we find a time when she isn't covering the desk.”
There is a short silence.
Then Daniel opens his calendar rather than arguing about the slot we already booked.

We spend the remaining time discussing things that are easy to overlook: a screen shared by two staff members, an afternoon shift that starts after the morning handover, the difference between receiving a message and being able to act on it.
Elena does not demand that we solve everything.
She asks us to stop describing the work as though everything has already been solved.
Before we finish, I read back my notes.
“You need a way to change class times without losing track of the people who still need contact.
You also need a manageable transition for staff.
Have I understood that correctly?”
“Yes.
